hook: "Green screen reaction ads are working really well right now. Here is the setup."
body: Antonioventre_ gives the green screen reaction ad setup: a base video plays — usually a creator or AI creator telling a story or talking about a problem — and a second person is greenscreened on top, reacting. The reactor comments on what's said or just confirms it: 'This worked for me too.' Why it hits: the viewer gets a double confirmation — one person makes the claim, a second person backs it up in real time. It feels less like an ad and more like watching someone vouch for it. The reactor can be real or AI.
idea: Two voices saying the same thing makes the product feel proven instead of pitched — the reactor is a live witness.
sequencing: The setup claim: working really well right now.
The base video: a creator or AI creator telling a story or problem.
The reactor layer: a second person greenscreened on top, reacting.
What the reactor does: comments, or confirms — 'This worked for me too.'
Why it hits: double confirmation — claim plus real-time witness.
The feel: vouching, not advertising.
The option: real or AI reactor.
why_it_works: Double confirmation is how humans actually decide — a claim plus an independent witness reads as proof, not pitch.
what_to_steal: LC's greenscreen reactor confirming a customer's waterproof story on camera: 'this worked for me too.'

hook: "Three ways we run native ads, all built on a long story in the primary text."
body: Antonioventre_ describes 3 native ad styles, all built on a long story in the primary text: (1) personal story — a real selfie and first-person story, feels like a friend posting, not a brand selling; (2) transformation story — before/after photo plus the whole journey, emotion keeps people reading; (3) doctor style — a nurse/doctor figure on a specific career case, driving to an advertorial with a short VSL. All three lead with emotion and a long story, never the product — the product shows up near the end, once people are hooked.
idea: Native ads lead with emotion and story — the product shows up near the end, once the reader is already hooked.
sequencing: Style 1: personal story — real selfie, first-person, feels like a friend posting.
Style 2: transformation story — before/after photo, the full journey, emotion keeps them reading.
Style 3: doctor style — a professional on a specific case, driving to an advertorial with a short VSL.
The rule: lead with emotion and a long story, never the product.
The payoff: the product appears near the end, once they're hooked.
why_it_works: The story creates a curiosity debt the product repays — by the time it appears, the reader wants the answer.
what_to_steal: LC's native template: first-person jewelry story in the primary text, product arriving at the two-thirds mark.

hook: "Green screen reaction ads are still one of our most reliable formats, and most brands build them wrong."
body: Antonioventre_'s correction on green screen reaction ads: most brands build them wrong. The setup is a base video (story, demo, AI explanation) with a creator greenscreened on top — pausing it, commenting, asking questions. The reactor's job is NOT to hype the product; it's to say what the viewer is thinking: 'No way this works.' ... 'Okay wait, that actually makes sense.' The reaction layer holds attention (two videos moving instead of one) and handles objections in real time through a person who sounds like the viewer, not the brand.
idea: The reactor is the viewer's proxy — they voice the objection, then get convinced on camera.
sequencing: The claim: still one of the most reliable formats; most brands build them wrong.
The setup: base video plays, creator greenscreened on top — pausing, commenting, questioning.
The reactor's real job: say what the viewer is thinking.
The example lines: 'No way this works.' → 'Okay wait, that actually makes sense.'
Mechanism 1: two moving videos hold attention.
Mechanism 2: objections handled in real time by someone who sounds like the viewer.
why_it_works: The viewer outsources their skepticism to the reactor — when the proxy converts on camera, they convert too.
what_to_steal: LC's reactor script verbatim in spirit: 'No way this is actually waterproof' → pause → 'okay wait, that actually makes sense.'

hook: "Secret of the DTC Universe #11: The Double 80/20 Rule in Creative Strategy"
body: Stefan Georgi's 'Double 80/20 Rule' post: his second massive winner in 21 days for an ecom brand cannibalized ad spend from his OG winner (~$750k in under three weeks). The angle had been declared 'doesn't work' for the brand — he ran it anyway, and it's heading for $1M+ in monthly spend. Takeaway: past performance is not indicative of future results; a winning ad is a strong idea meeting great execution. For yapper-style ads, execution means the creator, delivery, editing, pacing, and on-screen captions.

hook: "Native ads, end to end, for anyone who wants to build one"
body: Antonioventre_'s end-to-end native ad spec: the image — a normal-looking photo, a bit weird on purpose so people stop, with the problem in the picture (not the product). The first line of the primary text is the real headline — its only job is earning the 'See more' click. The copy: a first-person story from a situation the reader is in, product arriving around two-thirds down, 2,000-5,000+ words. Run it from a personal page, never the brand page. The lander: product page if they read the whole story, advertorial or listicle if they click early. Proof: $48.6K spent, $186K back, 3.83x ROAS.
idea: The complete native-ad spec: weird-problem photo, story-first copy, product at two-thirds, personal page — $48.6K to $186K at 3.83x.
sequencing: The image: normal-looking, a bit weird on purpose; the problem in the picture, not the product.
The first line: the real headline — its only job is the 'See more' click.
The copy: first-person story, product around two-thirds down, 2,000-5,000+ words.
The page: personal page for personal stories, theme page for articles — never the brand page.
The lander logic: full readers → product page; early clickers → advertorial/listicle.
The proof: $48.6K spent, $186K back, 3.83x.
why_it_works: Every element is engineered to delay the ad-frame — the click happens before the reader knows it's an ad.
what_to_steal: LC's native spec: weird-problem photo, first-person story, product at the 2/3 mark, run from a personal page.
